prompts:
This is an instructional notebook. It is notebook 3 of part 1 (regression on hourly bike rentals) of the course "Tabular Foundation Models with TabICL".

Content: removes a growing share of the weather readings (`weather`, `temp`, `feel_temp`, `humidity`, `windspeed`; calendar columns and the target stay complete) and measures how the error of HGBT and TabICL grows, with the usual 10-fold `TimeSeriesSplit` of 800/200 hours and a 48-hour gap. Values go missing completely at random (MCAR): one random number per cell, drawn once, so the holes at 25 percent are included in those at 50 percent and the curves compare nested sets of holes. At 100 percent the weather columns are dropped and the models predict from the calendar alone. TabICL uses `n_estimators=1`, so its errors on complete data differ slightly from the intro.

How each model copes: HGBT learns at each split whether rows with a missing value go to the left or right child, and treats a missing category as one more category. TabICL's internal preprocessing replaces a missing number by the training column mean with a `SimpleImputer`, and gives missing categories their own code through an `OrdinalEncoder`.

Results of the reference run: from complete readings to none, HGBT's mean MAE rises from 42 to 47 bikes per hour and TabICL's from 37 to 45; TabICL keeps the lower error at every fraction, with a gap below 2 at the end. HGBT's error peaks at 75 percent, so the last quarter of readings gives it nothing, while TabICL still gains about 2 bikes per hour from it. Error bars are wide and overlap, mostly because some test windows are harder.

Forward fill: since the weather changes slowly, the last past reading is a better guess than the column mean. A `FunctionTransformer` wrapping pandas `ffill`, restricted to the numerical columns by a column transformer with pandas output, is chained before TabICL with `make_pipeline`. It learns nothing in `fit`, only reads past hours, and works because training and test rows are in time order; holes at the very start of a test window stay empty and TabICL falls back to the mean. Results: at 25 percent, TabICL's MAE goes from 39.4 to 37.6 (37.1 on complete data); at 50 percent, from 41.9 to 39.4; at 75 percent, holes span several hours and the gain vanishes. The per-window paired gain is about 2 bikes per hour at 25 and 50 percent, with a standard deviation of about 6, driven by one window gaining 17 to 18. Never suggest imputations that read future hours (interpolation, backward fill).

Place in the course: after the learning curve; next comes the notebook on prediction intervals. Related scikit-learn course material: pipelines and column transformers (The Predictive Modeling Pipeline), histogram gradient boosting (Ensemble Models).
